ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Cell cycle control ensures cells divide only when needed; loss of regulation leads to uncontrolled proliferation and cancer. Clinicians must recognize patterns of dysregulation to guide diagnosis and therapy.

sections.p: Cell cycle control involves checkpoints (G1, S, G2, M) that monitor DNA integrity and growth signals. Diagnosis of dysregulation relies on histology, immunohistochemistry for p53, Rb, Ki‑67, and molecular tests for viral oncogenes.
b: Identify loss of p53 or Rb by IHC
Detect viral oncoproteins (HPV E6/E7, HTLV‑1 Tax)

t.b: Overexpression suggests TP53 mutation; absence may indicate viral degradation (HPV E6).
Reduced Rb points to HPV E7 activity or RB1 loss.
Positive confirms viral contribution to cell‑cycle loss.

sections.p: Tumors are staged by TNM; molecular grade adds prognostic value (e.g., p53 mutation = higher grade).
Most common cause is viral oncogenesis (HPV, HTLV‑1). Other causes include inherited mutations (Li‑Fraumeni), chemical carcinogens, and chronic infections prevalent in low‑resource settings.
b: HPV infection – genital warts, cervical cancer

sections.p: Patients may present with a mass, ulcer, or constitutional symptoms (weight loss, night sweats). In HPV‑related disease, lesions may appear as warts before malignant transformation.
Combine imaging, pathology, and molecular tests to confirm dysregulation and stage disease.

t.b: Defines tumor size and nodal involvement; if unavailable, use ultrasound.
High index (>20%) indicates rapid growth; low index suggests indolent behavior.
Positive confirms functional viral oncogene activity; if unavailable, rely on DNA PCR.

sections.p: Rapid growth, invasion of vital structures, metastasis, and paraneoplastic syndromes signal urgent intervention.
Treat the underlying cause first (e.g., antiviral therapy, surgical excision). Supportive care includes monitoring for tumor lysis and infection.
Regular surveillance with imaging and cytology (e.g., Pap smear for cervical HPV). Vaccination against HPV and HBV reduces future risk.
Benign proliferative lesions such as condyloma acuminata, reactive hyperplasia, or inflammatory granulomas can mimic malignant dysregulation.
p53 IHC can be falsely positive in wild‑type overexpression; low Ki‑67 may occur in small biopsies missing high‑grade areas.
b: False‑positive p53 due to fixation artifact

whenToSeekHelp: New onset severe pain or neurological deficit
Signs of metastasis (e.g., persistent cough, bone pain)

faq.a: HPV E6 degrades p53 and E7 degrades Rb, removing cell‑cycle checkpoints and allowing uncontrolled division.

faq.q: What is the role of p53 in the cell cycle?
faq.a: p53 halts the cycle for DNA repair or triggers apoptosis if damage is irreparable.

faq.q: How does HTLV‑1 contribute to leukemia?
faq.a: The Tax protein interferes with cell‑cycle regulators, promoting proliferation of infected T‑cells.

exam: Explain how HPV E6/E7 oncoproteins disrupt normal cell‑cycle checkpoints.
List three molecular tests used to identify cell‑cycle dysregulation and their clinical significance.
Describe management steps for a patient with HPV‑related cervical carcinoma, emphasizing why p53 status matters.
